statement.p: Suppose g is a function which has continuous derivatives, and that g(8)=-4, g'(8)=-3, g''(8)=-4, g'''(8)=2.
(a) What is the Taylor polynomial of degree 2 for g near 8?
(b) What is the Taylor polynomial of degree 3 for g near 8?
(c) Use the two polynomials that you found in parts (a) and (b) to approximate g(7.9).

static.solution:
g(x) = g(8) + g'(8)(x-8) + \frac{g''(8)}{2!}(x-8)^2 +\frac{g'''(8)}{3!}(x-8)^3+\cdots Substituting gives g(x) = -4 - 3(x-8) + \frac{-4}{2!}(x-8)^2 +\frac{2}{3!}(x-8)^3+\cdots
(a) The degree 2 Taylor polynomial, T_2 (x), is obtained by truncating after the (x-8)^2 term: T_2(x) = -4+\left(-3\right)\mathopen{}\left(x-8\right)+\frac{1}{2!}\mathopen{}\left(-4\right)\mathopen{}\left(x-8\right)^{2}.
(b) The degree 3 Taylor polynomial, T_3 (x), is obtained by truncating after the (x-8)^3 term: T_3 (x) = -4+\left(-3\right)\mathopen{}\left(x-8\right)+\frac{1}{2!}\mathopen{}\left(-4\right)\mathopen{}\left(x-8\right)^{2}+\frac{1}{3!}\cdot 2\mathopen{}\left(x-8\right)^{3}
(c) Substitute x=7.9 into the Taylor polynomial of degree 2: T_2(4.9) = -4+\left(-3\right)\mathopen{}\left(7.9-8\right)+\frac{1}{2!}\mathopen{}\left(-4\right)\mathopen{}\left(7.9-8\right)^{2} = -3.72. From the Taylor polynomial of degree 3, we obtain T_3(4.9) = -4+\left(-3\right)\mathopen{}\left(7.9-8\right)+\frac{1}{2!}\mathopen{}\left(-4\right)\mathopen{}\left(7.9-8\right)^{2}+\frac{1}{3!}\cdot 2\mathopen{}\left(7.9-8\right)^{3} = -3.72033.
